title: Let’s Not Make Reading a Wellness Trend
text:
A few weeks ago, I settled down on my couch to read Edith Wharton’s novel The House of Mirth on my iPhone. Or actually to reread—my friends had selected this old favorite of mine as a book-club pick, and our meeting was approaching. I was behind; life had gotten in the way of reading. I thought that I might just poke around for a few minutes to remind myself of the plot, but I was struck by the descriptions of the protagonist, Lily Bart, in the opening chapter—her strange combination of artifice and impulsivity. I had forgotten, or never registered, the moment when she says out loud that she would rather be happy than good. I put my phone down, did some things, and picked it up again to read. I lost track of time.

 But I didn’t really, because I was tracking myself using an app called Readwise Books. In that 40-minute “session,” I read roughly 136 words a minute. My “progress” was +2.1 percent of the novel as a whole. I was trying out “the Strava of reading,” as Readwise’s founders have described their creation—a reference to the popular running app that tracks speed, distance, heart rate, and other stats. These were my results.

 I n a n essay announcing the app last month , Readwise’s co-founders, Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi, ticked off a dizzying array of wellness fads and gadgets that have captured the public imagination in recent years: “Resistance training. Meditation. Cold plunges. Sauna (Finnish and infrared). Sleep tracking. Zone 2 cardio. VO2 max. Recovery. Ten thousand steps a day. Closing your rings. Standing not sitting. Continuous glucose monitors. Light exposure. Light blocking.” Doyon and Homsi posited that another practice should be included on the list, one backed by scientific evidence and known to increase well-being: “Reading books, of course.” They joined a growing chorus of people making the case that reading should be a wellness trend, a form of fitness for the mind—a sales pitch that struck me as new, and a little strange.

 [ From the August 2026 issue: The end of reading is here ] 

 Reading has long been considered a form of both moral and intellectual self-improvement. See, for instance, James Boswell’s The Life of Samuel Johnson , from 1791: “A young man should read five hours in a day, and so may acquire a great deal of knowledge.” More recently, figures including Oprah Winfrey have espoused reading’s benefits, among them “the way your mind is expanded when you’re exposed to new adventures and ideas.” And in the era of smartphones, many people have advocated for reading as an antidote to fraying attention spans. “Perhaps consuming a few dozen book pages a day should become the new 10,000 daily steps—a basic foundation of activity to maintain cognitive fitness,” the academic Cal Newport wrote earlier this year. This argument about reading and attention has an intuitive logic: Anyone who’s ever stopped scrolling and picked up a book can attest to the soothing, sharpening power of words on a page.

 But lately, these ideas have progressed into a case for reading’s value that sounds a lot like the way we talk about physical health. Some influencers are promoting reading alongside advice to eat whole foods and lift weights . The 75 Hard Challenge, a program that prescribes two 45-minute daily workouts, also tells participants to read 10 pages of a nonfiction book every day. Jon Finkel’s Books & Biceps newsletter explicitly marries the two. This month, Arnold Schwarzenegger’s weightlifting-focused newsletter included a plug for books, citing a study that showed readers of books had lower risk of mortality than those who didn’t read: “We can’t say that picking up a book will add years to your life. But it’s a low-risk behavior (really, there’s no risk in reading more) with high potential reward.” The point is no longer simply that reading is good for you in an amorphous, holistic sense; it’s that reading might increase your lifespan.

 This message is well suited for the age of ChatGPT. If going to the gym came into vogue after most American jobs moved away from manual labor, perhaps reading will do the same as more people offload cognitive work to generative AI. “People are coming to the realization that AI is doing more and more of the hard thinking that I used to do at work ,” Doyon told me. “ And my brain is starting to atrophy the same way my body atrophies by sitting in a chair .”

 And if reading really is the new Zone 2 cardio, it follows that you need a tracker for it, one that allows you to go beyond the traditional Goodreads metric of books per calendar year. In addition to words per minute and progress, Readwise—which is in an invite-only public beta mode but will be released to the wider public later this year—lets users see stats similar to those you might find in a sleep tracker. You can check if your reading has been “light,” or “active,” or “immersed.” (This feature is more experimental, Doyon said, and is based largely on how often people are highlighting phrases, looking up words, or taking notes.)

 I’m not sure, though, that tossing reading into the same good-for-you basket as eating your vegetables is a compelling pitch for an activity that already feels hard to many people. I expressed this reservation to Doyon, who reminded me that salad often actually tastes good. He said, “Working out feels good, right? It’s just hard to get into.”

 Doyon said that so far, Readwise seems to have two broad types of users. “There’s the group that’s in the self-improvement, quantified-self camp, and they like the data just because it’s got this aspect of self-discovery,” he said. The other group, he said, wants “keepsakes and mementos of activities they did. It’s kind of like taking a photo when you get to the top of a trail on a hike.” The data become a souvenir, something that can be shared with others.

 When I saw my stats for House of Mirth , though, I couldn’t make sense of them. Was 136 words per minute good, I wondered? I looked at the profiles of some of the other users, most of whom had higher WPM scores, many in the 200s. Well , I thought, isn’t Wharton’s prose more complicated than what you find in a contemporary self-help book? Wasn’t I reading slowly because I was savoring? And then: Why am I comparing myself at all? That can be one of the effects of tracking your activities—you suddenly find yourself in a race you’re not sure you signed up for.

 And reading is not running. I have run thousands of miles in my life—2,369.21 of which are recorded in my tracking app, the rest lost to history and shoddy data transfer. (Notice that even here, I’m subtly competing, telling you I’ve run more miles than the number captures.) The discipline involved in running is basically repetition: Get up; put your shoes on; get going; do it again. Of course, you run some memorable miles—hard ones, easy ones, fast ones, slow ones—but they are measurable and reducible to the same unit of distance. A mile is a mile, and your pace is the only thing that really changes. Over time, if all goes well, you get faster, or run farther, or both.

 [ Read: An underrated reason boys are reading less ] 

 Reading is defined instead by how nonlinear it is. Each time you pick up a book, your human mind interacts with one specific piece of art, written (one hopes) by someone with another singular consciousness. Books cannot be equalized. Stats such as words per minute—what can they tell you, really, about the experience of reading something, other than that it was fast or slow? I’ve read some of the least-rewarding books of my life in less than a day. Others, I inhaled quickly because I loved them so much. I’ve read slowly because I’m enjoying a long journey, or because a book is a slog. Data flatten these experiences. That’s what statistics do, in reducing experiences to their component parts. Books become pages become words. Put that number next to time spent reading, and as Doyon put it, “There’s an insatiable human impulse to divide them.”

 The subtext of quantified reading, of something such as 75 Hard’s prescription of 10 pages of nonfiction a day, is that you can push yourself to a reading goal in the same manner you can train for a marathon. I’m not sure that’s right, or, at least, I think it’s an approach that misses some of what’s best about reading.

 This is also why reading is an odd fit for the category of “wellness trends”—not because it doesn’t make you feel better, or because it can’t improve your mind, but because our general approach to wellness relies too much on the compression of experience. Reading is a fundamentally expansive activity. My graph of progress can’t tell me very much about losing myself in those familiar but forgotten chapters of House of Mirth , the magic trick of what language can conjure in your mind.
